lg.l: Amongst the eight [types of] marriage mentioned by prior theoreticians,
the kantiruvam custom is called kaḷavu.

div.p: eṉpatu kaikōḷ iraṇṭiṉ uḷḷuṅ kaḷavoḻukkām āṟuṇarttutaṉutaliṟṟu.

The quoted [cūttiram] intends to make known the way in which the clandestine-phase conduct occurs among the two [which form] kaikōḷ.This is not an easy phrase to translate, but it refers to the conduct appropriate to lovers in the clandestine and public phases of their relationship.
toṉ ṉūl āciriyarkaḷāṟ collap paṭṭa vaṟanilai yoppu poruḷ kōṭeyvam arum poruḷ vali nilai pēy nilai kantiruvam eṉap paṭṭa maṇam eṭṭiṉ uḷḷuṅ kantiruva vaḻakkam pōlvatu kaḷavoḻukkam ām eṉṟa vāṟu.

aṟanilai, oppu, poruḷ kōḷ, teyvam, arum poruḷ, vali nilai, pēy nilai, kantiruvam,These names are left untranslated here so the reader can clearly see the full Tamil enumeration. Each term has been translated in the following sections of the commentary. which are [all] mentioned by the teachers of the old treatises – amongst those eight [types of] marriage, the clandestine-phase conduct is the same thing as the kantiruvam custom.
aṟanilai yāvatu nāṟpatteṭṭiyāṇṭu piramacariyaṅ kāttāṟkup paṉṉīrāṭṭaip pirāyattāḷai yaṇikalam aṇintu koṭuppatu. iḵtoppil kūṭṭam ātaliṟ poruntāk kāmattiṉ pāṟ paṭum.

As for ‘the virtuous [marriage custom]’, [it is] the giving of a twelve-year-old girl, after being decorated with ornaments, to a protector who is a forty-eight-year-old brahmacarya. This is categorised as unsuitable love because this union is unequal.
oppāvatu maittuṉak kōttirattāṟku māṟṟātu koṭuppatu. itu kaṟpiṉ pāṟ paṭum.

As for ‘the consensual [marriage custom]’, [it is] the giving [of the bride] without refusal to the lineage of one’s maternal cousin. This is categorised as kaṟpu.This is a way to say that it is a type of marriage custom that is appropriate to the married phase in this poetic universe.
poruḷ kōḷ āvatu āṉum āṉ ēṟum poṟ kōṭṭup poṟ kuḷampiṉa vākac ceytavaṟṟōṭu nīriṟ koṭuppatu. ivvāṟōtaṟkaṇ otta pirāya mutal āyiṉ avaṟṟuḷaveṉiṟ kaṟpiṉ pāṟ paṭum. aṉṟeṉiṟ poruntāk kāmattiṉ pāṟ paṭum.

As for ‘the obtaining wealth [marriage custom]’, [it is] gilding the horns and hooves of a cow and bull and, along with them, giving [the bride] with water.This is a way to seal a contract in the dharmaśāstra-s. The cow and bull are part of the bride-price. This is implied, though not explicitly stated, in Gaut as well. In this way, on recitation [of the rites], if there is the basis of equal age and if those [other conditions]Gaut 1–5 list the conditions necessary for marriage: that the wife be of an appropriate caste; that she has not ‘belonged’ to another man; that she is younger than him; that they do not belong to the same precise ancestral lineage; and that they are not too closely related. exist, then this is categorised as kaṟpu. If not, then this is categorised as unsuitable love.
teyvam āvatu vēḷvi yāciriyarkku vēḷvit tī muṉṉar koṭuppatu. ituvum poruḷ kōḷōṭokkum.
As for ‘the divine [marriage custom]’, [it is] the giving [of the bride] to the sacrificial priest before the sacrificial fire. This too is the same as poruḷ kōḷ.
arum poruḷ viṉai yāvatu kol lēṟu taḻuvutal vil lēṟṟu mutalaṉa ceytārkkuk koṭuppatu. itu vaṉ maṇam ātaliṟ poruntāk kāmattiṉ pāṟ paṭum.

As for ‘the accomplishment of a difficult task [marriage custom]’, [it is] the giving [of the bride] to the one who has accomplished the embracing of the murderous bull, marksmanship, etc. This is categorised as unsuitable love because this is a forceful marriage.
vali nilai yāvatu tamariṉum avaḷiṉum peṟātu valintu koḷvatu. ituvum ataṉ pāṟ paṭum.
As for ‘the forceful [marriage custom]’, [it is] the forceful taking without obtaining [permission] from either her relations or from her. This too is categorised as that (being a forceful marriage).
pēy nilai yāvatu kaḷittāṇ māṭṭun tuyiṉṟāṇ māṭṭuñ celvatu. ituvum poruntāk kāmattiṉ pāṟ paṭum.

As for ‘the fiendish [marriage custom]’, [it is] the going [to the bride] when she is intoxicated or sleeping.I understand this as someone approaching the heroine while she is unable to consent – a euphemistic way to describe rape. This could also refer to someone going off with a woman while she is unable to consent. This too is categorised as unsuitable love.
kantiruvam āvatu ottār iruvar tāmē kaḷaviṉāṟ kūṭuṅ kūṭṭam.

As for kantiruvam,This is left untranslated as it is a proper name for a class of beings. If one wanted to, it could be translated as ‘celestial harpist’ or something similar. [it is] the union of two similar people through the clandestine phase [of love].

itaṉāl oruvāṟaṟamuṉ ākiya voppumai yuṭaittēṉum āṇ mutalākac collap paṭṭa kaḷavoḻukkan teyvap puṇarcciyum pāṅkaṟ kūṭṭamun tōḻiyiṟ kūṭṭattup pakaṟ kuṟiyum iravuk kuṟiyum varaivu kaṭātalum uṭaṉ pōkku valittalum eṉa vāṟām eṉṟa vāṟu. 14.

Therefore, even though it possesses an equality that has at its front the one virtuous path, the clandestine-phase conduct, which is said to begin with the man, is sixfold: the divine union; the union [by means of] his friend; the daytime tryst and the nighttime tryst [both being] of the union [by means of] her friend;In this enumeration, the two types of ‘the union [by means of] her friend’ are counted as individual items in the list. asking for marriage; and urging the elopement.

standOff.note: Cf. IA1: aṉpi ṉaintiṇaik kaḷaveṉap paṭuva | tantaṇa rarumaṟai maṉṟa leṭṭaṉuḷ | kantaruva vaḻakka meṉmaṉār pulavar ||
Cf. TP92n.3–5: kāmak kūṭṭaṅ kāṇuṅ kālai | maṟaiyōr tēettu maṉṟa leṭṭaṉuṭ | ṭuṟaiyamai nalyāḻt tuṇaimaiyō riyalpē ||

Cf. IAC1, p. 31: aṟanilai yoppē poruḷkō ṭeyvam | yāḻōr kūṭṭa marumporuḷ viṉaiyē | yirākkatam pēynilai yeṉṟik kūṟiya | maṟaiyōr maṉṟa leṭṭivai yavaṟṟuṭ | ṭuṟaiyamai nalliyāḻt tuṇaimaiyō riyalpitaṉ | poruṇmai yeṉmaṉār pulamai yōrē ||

The anonymous verse quoted in the IAC and cited as a source in the apparatus above is the earliest known enumeration of the ‘Tamil’ terms for the aṣṭavivāha (‘eight marriages’). Three Sanskrit attestations share the sequence found uniformly across the Tamil sources: the Gautama Dharmasūtra, the Arthaśāstra of Kauṭilya, and the Nāradasmṛti. Wilden (2021) argues that Kauṭilya and Nārada are the more probable sources for the transmission into Tamil, Nārada especially, since the Tamil treatment is in verse. The commentaries on Kauṭilya and Nārada that would have mediated this transmission are no longer extant, so the surviving evidence does not settle the choice between the three. I cite the Gautama Dharmasūtra in the apparatus because it is generally regarded as the earliest of the Dharmasūtras and so represents the earliest extant Sanskrit attestation of the list in the same sequence as the Tamil. The anonymous verse is also quoted in Iḷampūraṇar's commentary to the first cūttiram of the Kaḷaviyal (TP 92n). In essence, these names are really descriptions of the main characteristic of the marriage rite being performed. The other early enumeration we find for the eight types of marriage is also in the IAC, immediately following the above quoted verse. In this, Nakkīrar gives a correspondence between the Tamilised Sanskrit names of the types of marriage and the class of being for whom each type of marriage is suitable. For whatever reason, the TNV chooses the Sanskritic name for the marriage most appropriate for kaḷavu poetry – kantiruvam (Skt. Gāndharva) – as opposed to the Tamil term – nalyāḻt tuṇaimai (‘companionship of those with the good lutes’, i.e., the Gāndharva-s). For a more detailed analysis and explanation of the transmission of the aṣṭavivāha, see Wilden (2021).
There is no reason why the initial p in poruḷ would geminate, as in C1 and C2. These words are not compounded and there is no oblique case relation between them. They are enumerated items.

Cf. IAC1, p. 31: piramam eṉpatu nāṟpat teṭṭiyāṇṭu piramacariyaṅ kāttāṟkup paṉṉīrāṭṭaip pirāyattāḷai aṇikalaṉaṇintu koṭuppatu. koṭāviṭiṉ, orirutukkāṭci oruvaṉaic cārātu kaḻinta viṭattu oru pārppaṉakkolaiyōṭu okku meṉpatu; ataṉai aṟanilaiyeṉpatu.
Cf. Gaut4.6: brāhmo vidyācāritrabandhuśīlasaṃpannāya dadyādācchādyālaṃkṛtām
Cf. IAC1, p. 31: piracāpattiyam eṉpatu maittuṉa kōttirattāṉ makaḷvēṇṭic ceṉṟāl maṟātu koṭuppatu; ataṉai oppeṉpatu.
Cf. Gaut4.7: saṃyogamantraḥ prājāpatye saha dharmaś caryatām iti
Cf. IAC1, p. 31–32: āriṭam eṉpatu āvum āṉēṟum poṟkōṭṭup poṟkuḷampiṉavākac ceytu avaṟṟiṭai nīriṟkoṭuppatu; ataṉaip poruḷkōḷeṉpatu.
Cf. Gaut4.8: ārṣe gomithunaṃ kanyāvate dadyāt

UVC emended to ceytu avaṟṟōṭu, and I follow him. In C1’s reading, aṟṟōṭu in ceyvataṟṟōṭu (= ceyvatu aṟṟōṭu) functions as a sociative pronominalised demonstrative neuter singular, whereas the printed version is in the plural, and ceyvatu is a verbal noun and ceytu a viṉaiyeccam. In practice, the meaning of the passage remains the same with either reading. The source passage in the IAC, however, reads ceytu avaṟṟiṭai, and the editor notes a variant reading, avaṟṟōṭu. This strongly suggests that UVC’s emendation was correct, and that this was a standard description of this type of marriage. The rest of the description is almost identical. My hypothesis is that the C1 reading was the result of a scribal transposition, where the va eḻuttu and the ta eḻuttu were switched.
Cf. IAC1, p. 32: teyvam eṉpatu, vēḷviyāciriyaṟku vēḷvittīmuṉ vaittuk koṭuppatu; ataṉait teyvameṉṟu vaḻipaṭappaṭṭatu.
Cf. Gaut4.9: antarvedyṛtvije dānaṃ daivo ’laṃkṛtya
The same discrepancy between the honorific dative (-arkku) and the masculine singular dative (-aṟku) is reflected in different editions of the IAC. This edition simply follows C1.

The question of whether or not the consonant following muṉṉar geminates seems to be a marginal case, occurring slightly less often than not, based on what I found. As there is no gemination in C1, even though there is an error in the text that required correction, there is no gemination in this edition.

Cf. IAC1, p. 32: acuram eṉpatu, kollēṟu koṇṭāṉ ivaḷaiyeytum, villēṟṟiṉāṉ ivaḷaiyeytum, tiripiṉṟi eytāṉ ivaḷaiyeytum, mālai cūṭṭappaṭṭāṉ ivaḷaiyeytum iṉṉatoruporuḷ tantāṉ ivaḷaiyeytumeṉa ivvāṟu collikkoṭuppatu: aḵtu arumporuḷ viṉainilaiyeṉpatu.
Cf. Gaut4.11: vittenānatiḥ strīmatām āsuraḥ
Cf. IAC1, p. 32: irākkatam eṉpatu avaḷ taṉṉiṉun tamariṉum peṟātu valintu koḷvatu.
Cf. Gaut4.12: prasahyādānād rākṣasaḥ
Cf. IAC1, p. 32: paicācam eṉpatu mūttāṇmāṭṭun tuyiṉṟāṇmāṭṭuṅ kaḷittāṇmāṭṭuñ cārvatu: atu pēynilaiyeṉappaṭum.
Cf. Gaut4.13: asaṃvijñātopasaṃgamāt paiśācaḥ
Cf. IAC1, p. 32: kāntarvam eṉpatu iruvar ottār tāmē kūṭuṅkūṭṭam; ataṉai yāḻōr kūṭṭameṉpa.
Cf. Gaut4.10: icchantyāḥ svayaṃ saṃyogo gāndharvaḥ
